content: An epicanthal fold, also known as an epicanthic fold or epicanthus, is a fold of skin on the upper eyelid that extends from the nose to the inner side of the eyebrow, covering the inner corner of the eye (the medial canthus). This anatomical feature is commonly observed in individuals of East Asian descent, including ethnic groups such as Mongols, Turks, Chinese, Koreans, Japanese, Vietnamese, and others from East and Southeast Asia, such as Indonesians and Malaysians. It is also present in certain populations outside of Asia, including Inuit, some Indian groups, and the Khoisan people of Africa and Madagascar. Epicanthal folds can also be seen in young children of any ethnicity before the nasal bridge begins to elevate. The term epicanthal fold is a descriptive term based on appearance, but the underlying physiological reasons for its presence can vary significantly between individuals. All humans initially develop epicanthal folds during fetal development. Some children lose these folds by birth, but they may persist in young children of any ethnicity until the nasal bridge elevates. The folds are more likely to persist in cases of preterm birth or when the mother has a history of alcohol use during pregnancy. In some cases, epicanthal folds can create the appearance of crossed eyes, a condition referred to as pseudostrabismus. In individuals of Caucasian descent or other groups where epicanthal folds are not typically present, the presence of these folds can be associated with certain pathological conditions. These include fetal alcohol syndrome, chromosomal disorders such as Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), Cri du Chat syndrome, or preterm birth. Epicanthal folds are a common inherited trait in many populations, particularly among East Asian and Southeast Asian groups, though not universally. They are also found in significant numbers among Native Americans, the Khoisan of Southern Africa, many Central Asians, and some individuals of Sami origin. Additionally, they are prevalent in people of Tibetan descent, including Tibetans and certain North-East Burmese populations. Due to genetic inheritance patterns, children of a parent with a pronounced epicanthal fold and a parent without one may exhibit varying degrees of epicanthal folds. In East Asian populations, the presence of an epicanthal fold is often associated with a less prominent upper eyelid crease, commonly referred to as single eyelids, in contrast to double eyelids. However, these two features are distinct; an individual may have both an epicanthal fold and an upper eyelid crease, one without the other, or neither. The surgical procedure to reduce or remove epicanthal folds is known as epicanthoplasty. This procedure is now extremely rare. However, Asian blepharoplasty, a cosmetic surgery aimed at creating a double eyelid crease, remains a popular procedure in East Asia.
